The story section: this is the Sideshow move — you don't sell the product first, you sell the artist. Thirty years of feature animation is the reason a $35 ornament is a collectible and not a novelty. Numbers below animate up as they scroll in.

It started with
a pencil.

For three decades, Len Simon drew monsters, heroes and villains for the big screen — Anastasia, Titan A.E., The Prince of Egypt, Spirit, Curious George, Klaus. Thousands of drawings, every one made to move.

Then he wanted to hold them. So he started sculpting. And the first thing his hands made wasn't a hero. It was a fish with a grudge.

Process section (Apple-style): the left panel is pinned while the four steps scroll past on the right, each one swapping the image. Right now each step shows a character; the plan is a short looping clip of that actual step (sketch → clay → cast → paint). This is the section that turns "cheap ornament" into "art object" in a buyer's head.

01

The sketch

Every monster starts on paper, the way every character Len ever animated did. Dozens of drawings before one earns a face.

02

The sculpt

Clay, tools, and hours. Len sculpts the original by hand — the teeth, the wrinkles, the exact angle of a glare.

03

The cast

A mold is pulled from the original and every piece is cast in high-strength resin here in the shop. Heavy in the hand. Built to outlast the tree.

04

The paint

No two are identical, because every one is painted by hand at the bench. Eyes last. Always eyes last.
